section_summary: This section (pages 1–80) centers on an extensive September 1935 voluntary consular report by Richard F. Boyce, American Consul at Yokohama, and accompanying State Department memoranda analyzing the problems of second-generation Japanese Americans (Nisei) residing in Japan. Boyce examines their socio-economic backgrounds, the factors driving their migration—including the Great Depression and favorable exchange rates—as well as severe linguistic, domestic, and cultural adaptation difficulties. The section also catalogues educational institutions and social clubs catering to them, Japanese government efforts to orient them for cultural propaganda, and comprehensive enclosures including survey results, demographic statistics, a theatrical review, a Japan Cultural Forum membership roster, and the 1935 academic bulletin of the School of Japanese Language and Culture in Tokyo.

subfiles.about: A cross-reference document file note recording a voluntary report from Kobe concerning Japanese-American students in the Kobe consular district.
subfiles.from: Howard Donovan, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.summary: This document file note cross-references voluntary report number 150 Revision/188 from the American Consulate in Kobe, dated August 27, 1934, prepared by Consul Howard Donovan. It concerns students in Japan of Japanese race holding American citizenship. The referenced report includes a chart showing the number of Japanese-American students registered in the Kobe consular district and the ages at which they left the United States.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Kobe Voluntary Report: Students in Japan of Japanese Race and American Citizenship

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum summarizing and analyzing Consul Richard F. Boyce's voluntary report on second-generation Japanese of American citizenship in Japan.
subfiles.from: M. W. Schmidt, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: This memorandum from the Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviews Consul Richard F. Boyce's comprehensive thesis on second-generation Japanese of American citizenship residing in Japan. It analyzes the motivations driving these youth to Japan, including the U.S. economic depression, favorable currency exchange rates, and parental desires for cultural education. The memo notes the difficulties these youth face in adjusting to Japanese language and customs, their feelings of alienation, and the Japanese government's interest in orienting them favorably toward Japan to aid its cultural and political influence. It concludes that disillusioned returnees may counteract Japanese government propaganda upon returning to the United States and Hawaii.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Second-Generation Japanese of American Citizenship in Japan
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Consul Richard F. Boyce requests Department authorization to allow two Japanese American research assistants to read his voluntary report on second-generation Japanese in Japan.
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul at Yokohama
subfiles.summary: Consul Richard F. Boyce writes to the Secretary of State regarding his completed voluntary report on Americans of Japanese race residing in Japan. He explains that Miss Lily Mizuguchi of the Tokyo Y.W.C.A. and Miss Miya Sannomiya of the International Cultural Relations Association (Kokusai Bunka Shinkokai), both American citizens of Japanese descent, assisted extensively in preparing the report and requested permission to read it. Boyce expresses hesitation because their employers might wish to inspect or copy sections of the report. He requests Department approval and notes that, if granted, he would first remove the introduction and enclosures before sharing the text.
subfiles.title: Despatch on 'Second-Generation Japanese' in Japan: Permission for Research Assistants to Read Report

subfiles.about: A comprehensive voluntary report examining the social, economic, cultural, and political conditions of second-generation Japanese Americans living and studying in Japan.
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul at Yokohama
subfiles.summary: This voluntary consular report provides an extensive survey of American-born persons of Japanese descent (Nisei) residing in Japan, focusing especially on 'Group C' youth who grew up in the United States or Hawaii and moved to Japan after completing American schooling. Consul Boyce examines the factors driving their migration, such as the Great Depression, the favorable yen exchange rate, and family pressures, alongside the severe adjustment challenges they face regarding language barriers, unheated housing, diet, and social expectations. The report details their employment struggles, educational institutions established for them (such as the Y.M.C.A. School of Japanese Language and Culture, Waseda International Institute, and Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai), and social organizations like the Pacific Young People's Society and Japan Cultural Forum. Boyce also analyzes demographic and migration statistics, expatriation trends under Japanese nationality laws, and the geopolitical implications of Japanese government efforts to use second-generation Japanese for cultural propaganda.
subfiles.title: The Second-Generation Japanese Problem

subfiles.about: A supplementary report analyzing the Japanese government's interest in second-generation Japanese Americans and its broader cultural propaganda ambitions.
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul at Yokohama
subfiles.summary: This enclosure examines official Japanese policy toward second-generation Japanese, noting that the Japanese Foreign Office and other agencies have begun subsidizing educational institutions like the Kaigai Kyoiku Kyokai to cultivate favorable attitudes among visiting Nisei. Consul Boyce compares Japan's cultural expansion efforts to the Pax Romana, German Kultur, and Soviet world revolution, describing them as ambitious programs aimed at extending national political and economic influence under the guise of cultural dissemination. He observes that while spreading Japanese culture is not inherently objectionable, foreign governments must recognize these initiatives as state propaganda and monitor their effects.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1.(a): The Japanese Government [Government Aid to Second-Generation Japanese]

subfiles.about: A supplementary note discussing the minimal involvement of American resident communities and institutions in Japan with second-generation Japanese Americans.
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul at Yokohama
subfiles.summary: This enclosure describes the general lack of interest among American foreign colonies, business clubs, missions, and mission schools in Japan regarding second-generation Japanese Americans. While a few individual American missionaries, teachers, and Y.M.C.A. staff members actively assist the young people, the broader American resident community maintains little contact with them. Boyce notes that long-time American business residents would likely oppose admitting second-generation Japanese into established American clubs in Tokyo, Yokohama, and Kobe.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1.(b): Assistance from Americans in Japan

subfiles.about: A newspaper review of an English-language theatrical performance of Kikuchi Kan's samurai play 'Katakiuchi Ijyo' staged by the Pacific Young People's Society in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: This article from The Japan Times & Mail reviews a performance of Kikuchi Kan's three-act historical drama 'Katakiuchi Ijyo' (translated by Glenn Shaw as 'Better Than Revenge'), presented in English by the Pacific Young People's Society at Nippon Seinenkai-kan in Aoyama, Tokyo. The production, directed by Shiro Okakura with Professor Paul Rusch as production chairman, featured Satoru Sugimura in the lead role of Ichikuro alongside Himeko Nishikawa as Oyumi and Kazuo Ikeda. The review highlights the novel contrast between modern American-accented English and traditional Kabuki-style samurai drama, praising the cast's earnestness and success in raising funds for cultural study trips and research projects.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 3.(c): Famous Drama by Kikuchi Kan Given in English: American-Born Japanese Present Play of Samurai Era At Seinenkai-kan

subfiles.about: A survey questionnaire distributed to second-generation Japanese Americans living in the Tokyo-Yokohama area regarding their background, education, employment, and experiences in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This document reproduces the blank four-part questionnaire used by the Tokyo Y.W.C.A. and Consul Boyce to survey second-generation Japanese residing in Japan. Part I collects personal background details, including birthplace, birth date, parentage, and Japanese relatives. Parts II and III gather data on educational attainment in the United States and Japan, arrival dates, current employment, and future career intentions. Part IV investigates motivations for coming to Japan, difficulties in finding employment, perceived advantages of their American upbringing, and subjective feelings of happiness, loneliness, racial prejudice, and cultural adjustment.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 4.(a): Copy of Questionnaire

subfiles.about: Statistical compilation and analysis of survey responses from 104 second-generation Japanese Americans living in Japan collected by the Tokyo Y.W.C.A.
subfiles.summary: This enclosure compiles the tabulated results of the Tokyo Y.W.C.A.'s 1934–1935 census of second-generation Japanese, based on 104 completed returns (66 men and 38 women) out of 450 questionnaires distributed. It details respondents' birthplaces (predominantly California and Hawaii), birth years, American institutions attended, and current enrollment in Tokyo universities and schools. The compilation also summarizes major fields of study, present occupations (mostly students, followed by steno-typists and clerks), future intentions, and perceived advantages and obstacles in finding work. Furthermore, it records qualitative responses regarding what respondents appreciate about Japan (such as scenic beauty and freedom from race prejudice) and their grievances, including low living standards, lack of entertainment, police intrusiveness, and social alienation.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 4.(b): Results Taken from the Second Generation Census Taken by the Y.W.C.A. 1934 - 1935

subfiles.about: A roster listing seventeen prominent second-generation Japanese American members of the Japan Cultural Forum in Tokyo, detailing their occupations and American university degrees.
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul at Yokohama
subfiles.summary: This document provides a roster of seventeen members of the Japan Cultural Forum, an elite bilingual society of second-generation Japanese residing in Tokyo. Each entry lists the individual's current professional occupation in Japan and their alma mater in the United States or Canada. Members include journalists, physicians, research chemists, university lecturers, and consular employees affiliated with organizations such as the Japan Times, Shimbun Rengo, Riken (Institute of Physical and Chemical Research), St. Luke's Hospital, and the American Consulate at Yokohama.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 5: The Japan Cultural Forum Members

subfiles.about: The official 1935–1936 academic bulletin of the School of Japanese Language and Culture and the School for Foreign-Born Japanese operated at the Tokyo City Y.M.C.A.
subfiles.from: School of Japanese Language and Culture
keywords: School of Japanese Language and Culture
subfiles.summary: This published bulletin outlines the governance, faculty, academic calendar, and curriculum of the School of Japanese Language and Culture (Nichigo Bunka Gakkō) and its affiliated School for Foreign-Born Japanese, located at the Tokyo City Y.M.C.A. in Mitoshiro-cho, Kanda. It lists the Board of Trustees headed by Dr. Gilbert Bowles, advisory committees, administrative officers under Director Darley Downs and Honorary Director Baron Yoshiro Sakatani, and instructors. The publication details the school's direct teaching method, diploma requirements, tuition schedules, regular language courses, specialized religious courses for missionaries, an extension department for correspondence study, and diverse lecture offerings in Japanese art, history, political institutions, and customs.
subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2.(a): Bulletin of the School of Japanese Language and Culture (Nichigo Bunka Gakkō) with Which is Combined the Bulletin of the School for Foreign-Born Japanese
